name: Psychological Interventions
what: This subtopic examines two evidence-based psychological interventions for specific phobia: cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), which targets dysfunctional thoughts and behaviours, and systematic desensitisation, which uses graduated exposure paired with relaxation to extinguish the conditioned fear response.
why: Psychological interventions are heavily represented in VCAA exam questions. Both CBT and systematic desensitisation require detailed procedural knowledge and the ability to apply each to a novel case study with reference to the underlying psychological principles.

items.title: I can define cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) and identify its cognitive and behavioural components
items.what: Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) is a form of psychotherapy that encourages individuals to substitute dysfunctional cognitions and behaviours with more adaptive ones. The cognitive component involves identifying and replacing negative thoughts and feelings; the behavioural component involves identifying and replacing negative behaviours with healthier alternatives.
items.why: CBT is named in the study design as a psychological intervention and its two components must be correctly distinguished. Students who describe only the cognitive or only the behavioural component will not receive full marks on extended response questions.
items.example: A person with a phobia of driving works with a therapist to identify the thought 'I will definitely crash and die' (cognitive component: identify dysfunctional cognition) and replace it with 'statistically, most car journeys are completed without incident' (cognitive component: substitute adaptive cognition). They also begin taking short, low-speed drives rather than refusing all driving (behavioural component: substitute adaptive behaviour).

items.title: I can explain how CBT addresses the cognitive biases associated with specific phobia
items.what: CBT targets memory bias and catastrophic thinking by teaching the person to identify these distorted cognitions as hypotheses rather than facts, and to test them against evidence. A therapist guides the person to consider the statistical likelihood of feared outcomes and to recognise that their memories of traumatic events may be exaggerated.
items.why: The link between CBT as an intervention and the cognitive biases identified as contributing factors is an important conceptual connection. Exam questions may ask students to explain how CBT addresses a specific cognitive factor.
items.example: A person with arachnophobia who catastrophically thinks 'any spider I encounter will bite me and I will die' is asked by their CBT therapist to examine evidence: most spider species encountered in Australian homes are not venomous, and bites from those that are rarely cause serious harm. The person begins to treat the catastrophic thought as an overestimate rather than a fact.

items.title: I can explain how CBT addresses the behavioural components of specific phobia
items.what: The behavioural component of CBT targets avoidance behaviours that perpetuate the phobia through operant conditioning. A therapist works with the person to identify avoidance patterns and to replace them with gradual approach behaviours, reducing the negative reinforcement cycle that maintains the phobia.
items.why: Understanding that CBT addresses both cognition and behaviour, and that the behavioural component directly counters the operant conditioning perpetuation cycle, shows integrated knowledge across the topic.
items.example: A person with a phobia of social gatherings who cancels every social invitation (avoidance behaviour negatively reinforced by relief) works with their therapist to attend one small, low-stakes social event per week (adaptive replacement behaviour), reducing the reinforcement of avoidance and building tolerance.

items.title: I can define systematic desensitisation and describe its four steps
items.what: Systematic desensitisation is a therapy technique for overcoming phobia that involves incremental exposure to increasingly anxiety-inducing stimuli combined with relaxation techniques. The four steps are: (1) learning relaxation techniques, (2) developing a fear hierarchy, (3) gradual step-by-step exposure paired with relaxation, and (4) continuation until the most feared stimulus can be faced without a phobic response.
items.why: The four steps of systematic desensitisation are required procedural knowledge for the study design. VCAA exam questions frequently ask students to explain or apply the process of systematic desensitisation to a given phobia scenario.
items.example: For a person with a phobia of cats: (1) they learn breathing retraining; (2) they create a fear hierarchy from 'reading about cats' up to 'holding a cat'; (3) they begin with reading about cats while using breathing retraining until no fear is present, then progress to looking at cartoon cats, then photos, then videos, and so on; (4) they continue until they can hold a cat without a fear response.

items.title: I can explain how systematic desensitisation operates on the principles of classical conditioning
items.what: Systematic desensitisation is grounded in classical conditioning principles. The goal is to de-condition the association between the phobic stimulus (CS) and the fear response (CR) by repeatedly pairing the phobic stimulus with relaxation rather than fear. Over time, the phobic stimulus becomes associated with relaxation rather than terror.
items.why: The study design requires students to understand systematic desensitisation as a psychological intervention linked to classical conditioning. This connection ties the intervention directly to the precipitating contributing factor, demonstrating integrated understanding.
items.example: In a person with a phobia of dogs, the dog (CS) is currently paired with fear (CR) due to prior classical conditioning. In systematic desensitisation, the dog is gradually re-paired with relaxation responses (through breathing techniques applied at each hierarchy step) until the dog no longer elicits fear, replacing the conditioned fear response with a conditioned relaxation response.

items.title: I can compare CBT and systematic desensitisation as psychological interventions
items.what: Both CBT and systematic desensitisation are evidence-based psychological interventions classified as psychotherapeutic treatments. CBT addresses both the cognitive and behavioural dimensions of a phobia by modifying thoughts and behaviours, while systematic desensitisation specifically targets the conditioned fear response through incremental exposure and relaxation.
items.why: Comparison questions targeting both psychological interventions are common in the VCE Psychology exam. Students must identify at least one similarity and one meaningful difference.
items.example: Both involve working with a therapist to change how a person responds to their phobic stimulus (similarity). CBT directly challenges the person's thought patterns using cognitive restructuring (difference: cognitive component), while systematic desensitisation does not explicitly target cognitions but instead uses exposure to re-condition the fear response (difference: behavioural/conditioning mechanism).
